questions.why: Auquel, auxquels and auxquelles contract; à laquelle stays two words, exactly like au and à la.

questions.q: La table ___ j'ai posé mes clés. (on which)
questions.why: Table is feminine singular, and the preposition sur does not contract, so sur laquelle. French can never strand the preposition at the end.

questions.q: Le projet ___ je travaille. (the project I'm working on)
questions.why: Travailler à plus a masculine singular thing gives à + lequel, contracted to auquel.

questions.q: « La personne ___ je travaille. » Which is the natural choice?
questions.why: After a preposition, qui is the natural form for people. Avec laquelle is grammatical but heavier, and reserved for when you need to be unambiguous.

questions.q: « L'immeuble ___ j'habite. » — the building next to which I live.
questions.why: Dont covers a plain de. When the de is buried inside a compound preposition (à côté de, au-dessus de, près de), you must switch to duquel.

questions.q: Le film ___ je parle. (the film I'm talking about)
questions.why: Parler de is a plain de, so dont. Duquel here would be wrong, and heavy.

questions.q: Le pays ___ je viens. (the country I come from)
questions.why: For place and time, où is lighter than lequel and generally preferred. Venir de plus a place gives d'où, not duquel.

questions.q: Build the phrase: the pen I write with.
questions.why: The preposition and the pronoun stay welded together at the front of the relative clause. There is no French sentence ending in avec.

questions.q: Je ne sais pas ___ se passe. (what's going on)
questions.why: No noun antecedent, and the pronoun is the subject of se passe, so ce qui. If it were the object, it would be ce que.

questions.q: C'est ___ j'ai besoin. (that's what I need)
questions.why: Avoir besoin de takes de, and with no noun antecedent the de form is ce dont.

questions.q: « C'est ___ je pense. » — that's what I'm thinking about.
questions.why: Penser à takes à, and with no noun antecedent à becomes ce à quoi. Ce dont would go with penser de, which means to have an opinion of.

choices: Il est parti, qui m'a surpris.
Il est parti, ce qui m'a surpris.
Il est parti, que m'a surpris.
Il est parti, dont m'a surpris.
questions.why: The antecedent is the whole preceding idea, not a noun, so it must be ce qui. This is the French for the English which that comments on a clause.

questions.q: Type what you hear, in correct written French.
questions.why: For a place, où beats dans laquelle every time. Note the accent: où is where, ou is or.

questions.q: Say this out loud: the project I'm working on.
questions.why: English strands the preposition at the end; French puts it first, fused into auquel.

questions.q: You need a relative pronoun. Give the questions you ask yourself, in order, to pick the right one.
a: 1. Is there no noun antecedent, just an idea? Then ce qui / ce que / ce dont / ce à quoi. 2. Is the preposition a plain de? Then dont. 3. Is it a place or a time? Then où. 4. Another preposition, and a person? Then qui. 5. Another preposition, and a thing? Then lequel and its contractions. 6. No preposition at all: subject qui, object que.
questions.why: The choice is mechanical once you ask about the antecedent and the preposition in that order.
